name: Motown
ownershipStory: Berry Gordy founded Motown (first as Tamla) in Detroit in January 1959, converting a photography studio at 2648 West Grand Boulevard into the Hitsville U.S.A. studio and headquarters. Gordy ran the label like a factory: staff songwriters, a house band, and weekly quality-control meetings where he personally vetoed any single he judged wouldn't compete with that week's top five pop records. Gordy sold his stake to MCA Records and Boston Ventures for $61 million in 1988; the label passed to PolyGram in 1993 and then to Universal Music Group in 1999, which still owns it.
hook: A converted Detroit photography studio that ran hit singles through a factory process strict enough that Berry Gordy personally vetoed anything that wasn't good enough.

blurb.age13: Berry Gordy started Motown in Detroit in 1959, turning a small photography studio into Hitsville U.S.A. He ran it like a factory: staff songwriters wrote for whichever act suited a song best, a house band played on almost everything, and Gordy held a meeting every week where he personally decided which songs were good enough to release.
blurb.adult: Motown's assembly-line production system, criticized by some as impersonal and celebrated by others as a genuine hit-making discipline, is the clearest example on this map of a label's internal process, not just its contracts or distribution, directly shaping what got released and to whom a song went.
